That means GCC's default fast mode and nvcc's host compilation both apply FMA-contraction during input generation, while the strict ISO build doesn't — confirming nvcc's host side behaves like gnu-fast mode. So the divergence I'm chasing now is really about how the decomposition step gets contracted differently between the GPU's no-fma path and the CPU's fast-math path.\n\nRather than keep fighting the ambient compiler flags, I'm going to isolate just the decomposition function and force strict IEEE behavior on it specifically — tagging it with a function attribute to disable fp-contract just for that routine, while leaving generation under normal fast-math. {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1792955590540,"sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","part":{"id":"prt_1747ac8e0001ilU3K3ujIv7632","messageID":"msg_1747ac3d3001YN91rfGpJi6jLb","sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","type":"reasoning","text":"The update kernel averages 156us while diag takes 34us running 256 threads per column. I'm realizing the real bottleneck: for a column with j≈1000, only 1000 threads spin up across 4 blocks, meaning just 4 SMs out of 82 get used—massive underutilization of the GPU.\n\nEach thread's serial chain through j iterations is long since the independent work per column (n-j dot products) is inherently limited in parallelism. The real fix is pipelining multiple columns as a wavefront, where a thread per row processes columns in sequence, only blocked by dependencies on the diagonal and prior column results—letting rows progress concurrently instead of column-by-column.\n\nThis requires a persistent kernel with global-memory flags and spin-waiting to coordinate row threads, ensuring diagonal values are ready before dependent rows can proceed—complex to implement correctly with co-residency constraints across SMs, but feasible for reasonable matrix sizes.\n\nRow i's step j must wait until row j completes its own diagonal, so the timeline has row j finishing at roughly time proportional to j, and row i's progress chains behind that. The critical path ends up similar to before, roughly O(n²) total work since each row's step j still involves a serial dot-product of length j, even though rows now run concurrently.\n\nThe wavefront approach really halves the critical path versus the current method, since it removes the separate serial update phase, but the inherent dependency chain of length j for column j's dot product remains fundamental. For n=2048, that works out to roughly 2M chain-latency units, or around 8M cycles minimum assuming FMA and load latencies, giving a theoretical floor of about 4ms.\n\nThe real culprit at 415ms—roughly 100x above that floor—is unhidden memory latency: each global load takes 400-600 cycles, and with only a handful of SMs active and limited loads in flight per warp, we're not getting enough memory-level parallelism to amortize that. Boosting unroll depth or staging data in shared memory with bulk cooperative loads across a tile of rows could close that gap significantly.\n\nWorking through the ideal case: with j-length dependent chains using shared memory (~4-8 cycles per step after staging), the parallel width across a column is still only n-j rows, so for large n the SM count outstrips available parallelism per column. The real bottleneck becomes chain latency itself—around 4000 cycles per column—giving a theoretical floor near 4ms total plus kernel launch overhead pushing it to roughly 12ms, which means the 1M FMAs per column need to be spread across all 82 SMs with each SM handling a dozen or so long chains.\n\nI'm reasoning through staging global memory into shared memory tiles: threads cooperatively load column chunks of L coalesced by row index, sync, then each thread chains through C FMAs locally from smem, which keeps total global memory traffic at roughly n³/6 × 8 bytes, around 1.4GB for n=2048.\n\nWorking through latency estimates, I figure chunk size C=32 with 128-thread blocks gives roughly 31 round trips of ~500 cycles per column, totaling around 8us per column and ~8ms overall versus the current 415ms, a ~40x speedup. A simpler alternative might be using a #pragma unroll of 32 independent loads per thread to let the compiler achieve memory-level parallelism without the smem bookkeeping, and I'd want to check whether ptxas actually schedules those loads early. I should also test applying the same unrolling trick to the diagonal kernel, which currently takes ~34us per call and ~69ms total, since its smem loop could similarly benefit from hiding latency behind unrolled FMA chains.\n\n","time":{"start":1792955566304,"end":1792955590435},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1792955686015,"sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","part":{"id":"prt_1747c7ab2001KNOi6xYSfQmTmq","messageID":"msg_1747c73df0011ya4A3fF8zz0GR","sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","type":"reasoning","text":"The unrolling isn't helping, which makes me suspect the compiler isn't hoisting the loads due to aliasing concerns around the restrict pointer, or possibly the __dadd_rn intrinsic is interfering with instruction scheduling even though the loads themselves should still be reorderable.\n\nI'm estimating bandwidth: the strided reads of LT per column should be coalesced fine, and total data volume for the update phase (~14GB across all columns) would only need ~15ms at full DRAM bandwidth, nowhere near the ~400ms observed, so raw memory throughput isn't the bottleneck. Working the numbers per-thread suggests only ~9 billion loads/second are being achieved, which points toward insufficient parallelism — too few active blocks/threads to hide latency — rather than a memory bandwidth ceiling.\n\nWith only up to ~2048 active threads and each one issuing a single dependent load per iteration at roughly 500ns latency, the achievable throughput works out to almost exactly the observed ~4.4 billion iterations/second, confirming the kernel is latency-bound because each thread has only one load in flight rather than multiple overlapping ones. That suggests the compiler isn't actually unrolling the load instructions despite the pragma — possibly due to unknown trip counts, aliasing concerns with the later store, or the intrinsic calls blocking reordering — so I'm thinking the fix is to manually prefetch values into registers ahead of use rather than relying on the compiler to do it.\n\n","time":{"start":1792955677362,"end":1792955685890},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1792955742132,"sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","part":{"id":"prt_1747d04d5001Qs4qggXauXkDvu","messageID":"msg_1747d00be001vyfqHbaGwu7mEL","sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","type":"reasoning","text":"The hash matches for n=1000 but timing is unchanged at 413ms, so loading latency isn't the bottleneck. I'm wondering if FP64 throughput is the real constraint, since the RTX 3090 only runs double precision at 1/64 rate compared to single precision.\n\nWorking through the numbers, theoretical peak DP throughput would only need about 5-10ms for the total FLOPs involved, so that's not the limiter either. I think the real issue is that without fused multiply-add, each iteration requires two separate DP operations, and with only 2 DP units per SM on Ampere, the chip-wide throughput works out to roughly 82 iterations per cycle — which when divided into the 1.4 billion total iterations starts to explain the much larger observed runtime.\n\nThat's roughly consistent with the 320ms number once overhead and underutilization are factored in — if fully spread across all 82 SMs it'd be closer to 10ms, so the real bottleneck is the 3090's weak FP64 throughput combined with poor SM occupancy. To speed things up I need to get more SMs busy, meaning more parallel work per launch, likely by distributing across columns in a wavefront pattern.\n\nThe core issue is that the active thread count per column is capped at roughly n-j, so for n=2048 that only fills about 8 SMs out of 82 — the column-wise parallelism strategy is inherently limited regardless of block size. The way around this would be running multiple columns concurrently through pipelining to actually occupy the rest of the SMs.\n\nA wavefront approach where rows are processed concurrently with flag-based synchronization could spread the 1.4 billion DP operations across all 82 SMs, dropping runtime to maybe 10-20ms — roughly a 20x speedup — but it requires a persistent kernel with spin-flags, which is fragile. I'm also considering whether column j+1's update could reuse the same thread that just finished column j's update for that row, enabling a skewed schedule across kernel launches instead.\n\nWorking through the dependency timing: scheduling row i's work on column j at step t(i,j) = i+j satisfies both the sequential column dependency and the diagonal dependency, giving an anti-diagonal wavefront with about 2n steps total — same launch count as before, but now each step processes up to n/2 independent entries in parallel instead of just one.\n\nStill, the width per step tops out around n/2 (roughly 1024 threads, keeping only ~8 SMs busy), and the critical path per step is still proportional to the entry's column index j, so this wavefront approach doesn't actually beat the simple column-by-column scheme in terms of concurrency — the real bottleneck is that each element's dependency chain has length j, and there's no way around that serial depth without changing the algorithm itself.\n\nThis essentially forms a wavefront pattern giving roughly O(n) kernel steps with many (i,j) chains running concurrently. Given GPU shows 415ms vs CPU's 2142ms (5x speedup) at n=2048, the real bottleneck is parallel width per column constrained by the RTX 3090's throughput and the need for bit-exact ordering.\n\nI'm considering whether a row-thread approach could help: each thread for row i processes columns j=0 to i-1 sequentially, since update(j+1) for a row only depends on that same row's update(j) completing, so a single thread could chain through columns without waiting on other rows' column updates.\n\nSo total wall time ends up scaling like n²/2 iterations per thread, which for n=2048 means roughly 2M serial iterations per thread — but since n=2048 threads are active concurrently, that's again only 8 SMs worth of parallel width, so the dependency chain still dominates.\n\nThe real issue is that splitting work by row means each row's columns form a sequential chain, since computing L[i][j] depends on L[i][j-1] through the dot product — so I can't trivially assign multiple threads to the same row without breaking that dependency, which limits how finely I can spread work across all SMs.\n\nTo actually hit that ideal timing, I'd need to exploit concurrency across elements that don't depend on each other—like elements along the same anti-diagonal across different rows, since each individual dot product can't be split further but independent elements can run in parallel.\n\nWith row-pipelining and fine skewing, concurrency could scale up toward n threads, roughly 2048 for n=2048, which maps to 64 warps distributed across 8 SMs. But I need to account for the DP-throughput ceiling per SM, and whether FMA fusion is allowed changes whether each iteration costs one or two DP ops, affecting the achievable speedup by roughly 2x.\n\nWorking through the actual timing: with 2 DP lane-ops per cycle per SM and 1.4e9 iterations needing 2 ops each, the total lane-ops divided by 82 SMs at 2 ops/cycle gives roughly 17 million cycles, about 9 ms if fully utilizing all SMs. But with only 2048 threads spread across 82 SMs, that's just 25 threads per SM, not enough to hide the multiply-add dependency chain latency (roughly 16 cycles per iteration), so the DP pipeline likely can't stay saturated with so few threads per SM.\n\nSo the real fix is spreading the same 2048 threads across many more SMs by using smaller thread blocks -- say 32 or 64 threads per block instead of 256 -- since the scheduler distributes blocks breadth-first across SMs. With 64 blocks of 32 threads, we'd hit 64 SMs instead of just 8, cutting the estimated time from roughly 415ms down to around 12ms. {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1792955901493,"sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","part":{"id":"prt_1747f9495001lF5qsL8WedVtju","messageID":"msg_1747f8f630016lcf7u2s62JtV9","sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","type":"reasoning","text":"The 250ms seems dominated by the update kernel rather than the diagonal one, so I should profile the batch-16 build again to see the actual time split, and think through the memory access pattern per column to understand the DRAM bottleneck in the update step.\n\nWorking through the bandwidth math, the total data read across all columns comes to roughly 14GB, which at full 3090 bandwidth would only take about 15ms — so pure DRAM bandwidth isn't the bottleneck for the 180ms observed. That points me toward latency or occupancy issues instead, possibly compounded by the overhead of 64-bit index arithmetic (like computing flattened array offsets) which can expand into multiple instructions on the GPU.\n\nI estimate the double-precision throughput on this consumer GPU is severely limited (roughly 1/64 the FP32 rate), giving a DP-bound floor of about 10ms — still far below the 180ms actually seen, so that's not the bottleneck either. I consider trying nsys/ncu profiling and switching to 32-bit indices as experiments, then weigh whether current performance (~8x speedup at n=2048, but no gain at n=512 due to kernel launch overhead) is good enough given time constraints.\n\nI'm now thinking through a more aggressive pipelined approach: launching a single kernel that handles multiple diagonal/column steps together so threads can advance sequentially through dependent steps without separate kernel launches for each step, which could reduce launch overhead significantly but adds real complexity and risk.\n\nThis single-block trick is cheap but limits throughput to one SM, so it's great for small n (≤1024) but doesn't scale. For large n like 4096, the column-wise width grows to 4096, requiring many more blocks, which exposes the real tension: the algorithm's strict ordering constraints cap how much parallelism I can extract.\n\nAt that scale, though, I'd also need to worry about CPU-side matrix generation time becoming a bottleneck, since the exact bit-reproducible random generation is itself O(n^3). Estimating the theoretical DP-bound cycle count for n=4096 suggests an ideal runtime around 150ms, but my current design is probably closer to a couple seconds, so there's still a meaningful gap to the theoretical floor.\n\nGiven the effort constraints, I'll settle for moderate optimizations: using a block size of 32 or 64 for the update step, batching loads, and considering whether indices can safely use 32-bit unsigned arithmetic instead of 64-bit size_t. I'm working out that since memory limits on a 24GB GPU already cap n well below the point where n² would overflow 32-bit unsigned range, I could use unsigned ints safely, but to stay correct for any theoretical n, it's safer to keep 64-bit pointer arithmetic and just increment row pointers by n each iteration, which should be cheap.\n\nNow I'm analyzing the diagonal kernel's cost: with a single thread doing sequential dot-product accumulation across smem-staged chunks, the latency chain dominates, giving roughly 20ms in theory but 70ms in practice. I'm considering whether diagonal computation for column j+1 could overlap with the update step for column j, but concluding it can't since it depends on that update's output for the next row, so the sequencing has to stay as is — though I could still try to shorten the per-thread multiply-add latency chain by offloading part of the squaring work to other threads.\n\nI'm planning to have all threads compute their products in parallel into shared memory, since multiplication order doesn't affect bit-exact results, leaving thread 0 to just sum them — cutting the serial chain roughly in half. The same idea applies to the update step's dot products, since the multiplications there are independent of the running sum. I want to implement this staged-product approach along with testing different thread batch sizes and pointer increment strategies, then benchmark the results.\n\n","time":{"start":1792955880597,"end":1792955901479},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

products are formed with explicit rounding (no FMA).\n// Loads are batched so that several memory requests are in flight per thread.\n__global__ void updateKernel(double* __restrict__ LT, size_t n, size_t j) {\n    const size_t i = j + 1 + (size_t)blockIdx.x * blockDim.x + threadIdx.x;\n    if (i >= n) return;\n\n    const double* pa = LT + i; k < j; ++k) {\n        sum = __dadd_rn(sum, __dmul_rn(*pa, *pb));\n        pa += n;\n        pb += n;\n    }\n    LT[j * n + i] = (LT[j * n + i] - sum) / LT[j * n + j];\n}\n\n'''\ns=s[:start]+upd+s[end:]\ns=s.replace('constexpr int UPDATE_THREADS = 256;','constexpr int UPDATE_THREADS = 32;\\nconstexpr size_t UPDATE_BATCH = 16;')\n# 2) diagonal: products computed in parallel, thread 0 accumulates in order\nds=s.index('// Computes the diagonal element of column j.')\nde=s.index('// Computes column j below the diagonal')\ndiag='''// Computes the diagonal element of column j. (j - base) : DIAG_CHUNK;\n        for (size_t t = threadIdx.x; t < len; t += blockDim.x) {\n            const double v = LT[(base + t) * n + j];\n            sq[t] = __dmul_rn(v, v);\n        }\n        __syncthreads();\n        if (threadIdx.x == 0) {\n#pragma unroll 8\n            for (size_t t = 0; t < len; ++t) {\n                sum = __dadd_rn(sum, sq[t]);\n            }\n        }\n        __syncthreads();\n    }\n\n    if (threadIdx.x == 0) {\n        const double val = LT[j * n + j] - sum;\n        if (val <= 0.0) {\n            // Matrix is not positive definite; {"type":"reasoning","timestamp":1792956009806,"sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","part":{"id":"prt_17481599e001YCX2z3iIVM7rL1","messageID":"msg_17481552a001f4s7nohsnLc4Ee","sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","type":"reasoning","text":"I'm questioning whether the 32us diagnostic timing and 77us update timing actually make sense given the amount of work being done—trying to sanity-check if strided loads and loop iterations account for the measured latency.\n\nLooking more carefully, the real bottleneck seems to be occupancy: with only (n-j) threads per column, we end up with just one warp per SM for smaller columns, so the GPU's parallel width is capped far below its capacity, which would explain the slower-than-expected timings from memory latency dominating a single warp's iterations rather than being hidden by other warps.\n\nThe real fix is pipelining across columns rather than reducing per-warp latency. I'm considering whether a row-thread could compute two adjacent columns in sequence, since row i's update for column j+1 depends on L[i][j] which it just computed itself, while the diagonal pivot for j+1 depends on another thread's output — so I'm sketching a kernel structure where thread i handles column j for all rows below the diagonal and also feeds into the next column's computation.\n\nThis requires a grid-wide synchronization between columns, which cooperative groups could provide, but the per-column sync cost is comparable to launch overhead and doesn't actually increase the available parallel width — the fundamental constraint remains that only n-j chains of work exist at column j, and fusing adjacent columns doesn't widen that since the chains within a row are inherently sequential.\n\nGiven time constraints, I'll accept the current ~8.5x speedup for n=2048 and move on, noting that at n=512 the gains basically vanish since launch overhead, memory allocation, and synchronization costs dominate the tiny amount of actual work — that's a limitation worth mentioning rather than chasing further.\n\nI'm also weighing whether to tune block size and batch parameters further for the v3 kernel, but the diagonal serial dependency chain (roughly 8 cycles per dependent FP64 add times ~1024 iterations) already explains most of the per-column latency, so additional micro-tuning likely yields diminishing returns given how much time I've already spent.\n\n","time":{"start":1792955996574,"end":1792956009746},"metadata":{"anthropic":{"signature":""}}}}

{"type":"text","timestamp":1792956305053,"sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","part":{"id":"prt_1748601380015bPR2ROliTokgD","messageID":"msg_17485fbbc001j3hm0qlAV3nS54","sessionID":"ses_e8b964d13ffewE7B2dosKjP6jw","type":"text","text":"The Cholesky decomposition now runs on the GPU through CUDA, and the executable is still `cholesky`. It is bit-identical to the original's decomposition when that is compiled without FMA contraction. Speedups over the original binary are about 2x at n=512, 4.6x at n=1024, and 8.7x at n=2048.\n\nOnly `cholesky/cholesky.cpp` and `cholesky/CMakeLists.txt` changed. No new files were created.\n\n**Approach**\n- The original's dot products are summed sequentially in `k`. To keep that order, the GPU runs one column at a time. For each column, a diagonal kernel computes `L[j][j]`, then an update kernel computes all rows below it in parallel.\n- Device data is column-major so that warps read contiguous memory.\n- Matrix generation and `-v` validation stay on the CPU, as in the original, so their results are unchanged. The timed region still covers allocation, transfers, and the decomposition.\n- A non-positive pivot still prints the same error message and returns failure. `initCudaDevice()` creates the CUDA context before timing starts.\n\n**Build**\n- The project uses `LANGUAGES CXX CUDA`, and `cholesky.cpp` is compiled as CUDA.\n- `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES` is `native`, which requires CMake 3.24 or later and a GPU present at configure time. I verified it with CMake 3.30, CUDA 12.0, and an RTX 3090 (sm_86).\n\n**Numerical note**\n- The device code uses explicit `__dmul_rn`/`__dadd_rn` instead of FMA. This matches the source compiled with `-ffp-contract=off`. The original default build (GCC `gnu++20`, `-march=native`) contracts some operations into FMA, so its `-r` hash differs in the last bits. I could not reproduce GCC's exact contraction pattern on the GPU.\n- Results match the reference hashes at every size tested, from n=0 to 2048. `-v` validation passes.\n\n**Limits**\n- The column order exposes only about `n-j` independent dot products per launch, which is what caps the speedup. Going further would need a multi-column pipeline with cross-block synchronization.\n- For n=4096, the CPU-side matrix generation takes minutes, which dominates total runtime. It is outside the timed region, but it is still O(n³) on the CPU.","time":{"start":1792956301624,"end":1792956305049}}}
